chapters.title: Vernier calipers: read and correct
chapters.formula: Reading = main-scale reading + coincidence number x least count - zero error
points: Outer jaws measure external diameter; inner jaws measure internal diameter.
The depth rod measures vessel depth when correctly aligned.
For 10 VSD = 9 MSD with 1 MSD = 1 mm, least count is 0.1 mm.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. Experimental questions become much easier when you understand what the instrument is actually measuring. Vernier calipers have outer jaws for external dimensions, inner jaws for internal dimensions, and a depth rod for the depth of a vessel. Choose the right contact surfaces, align the instrument, and use gentle contact rather than squeezing the object. Before measuring, close the clean jaws and check the zero. For a direct vernier with ten vernier divisions matching nine main-scale divisions, one vernier division is zero point nine millimeters when a main-scale division is one millimeter. Their difference, zero point one millimeters, is the least count. Read the main-scale mark immediately to the left of the vernier zero. Then find the vernier mark that coincides with a main-scale mark. Add that coincidence number times the least count. Here is our original example: the main-scale reading is two point three centimeters, the seventh vernier mark coincides, and least count is zero point zero one centimeters. The raw reading is two point three seven centimeters. If the closed jaws show positive zero error of zero point zero three centimeters, subtract it. The corrected result is two point three four centimeters. Pause and check the sign: zero correction is negative zero error. Repeat readings at different positions to detect uneven diameter, and avoid parallax when judging alignment. Least count tells you resolution; it does not automatically guarantee the same absolute accuracy.

chapters.title: Screw gauge: pitch, ratchet and backlash
chapters.formula: Least count = pitch/circular divisions; corrected reading = sleeve + circular contribution - zero error
points: Pitch is axial travel in one complete screw revolution.
Use the ratchet for consistent contact force.
Approach the reading in the same direction to reduce backlash error.
chapters.script: A screw gauge converts rotation into a small linear movement. Pitch is the distance the spindle advances in one full revolution, not the total length of the screw. If pitch is zero point five millimeters and the circular scale has fifty divisions, least count is zero point zero one millimeters. Take the visible sleeve reading, including an exposed half-millimeter mark when appropriate, then add the circular-scale reading times least count. In our example, the sleeve shows one point five millimeters and the circular reading is twenty-eight. Add zero point two eight millimeters to obtain a raw reading of one point seven eight millimeters. Suppose zero error is negative zero point zero two millimeters. Corrected reading is raw reading minus that negative error, giving one point eight zero millimeters. Keep the trailing zero because it communicates the stated resolution. A ratchet helps apply consistent light contact instead of crushing a wire or sheet. Backlash is slack between the screw and nut that can make reversing rotation misleading. Approach the final contact in the same rotation direction, following the instrument's procedure. If you overshoot, back off sufficiently and approach again; do not treat a tiny reversal as guaranteed real spindle movement. Check zero before and after a set of measurements, and measure a wire at different locations and orientations. One last trap: if a question gives diameter but a later equation requires radius, divide by two before squaring. The instrument reading and the derived quantity are separate steps.

chapters.title: Find an unknown mass using moments
chapters.formula: About the balance point: mknown dknown = munknown dunknown
points: First locate the empty metre scale's center of gravity.
Distances are measured from the pivot, not from a scale end.
If the pivot is elsewhere, include the scale's own weight moment.
chapters.script: Now a metre scale becomes a balance. First find where the empty scale balances horizontally on a narrow support. That point identifies its center of gravity; do not assume every real scale balances exactly at fifty centimeters. Suspend a known mass on one side and an unknown mass on the other. If the pivot is at the scale's center of gravity, the scale's own weight has zero moment about the pivot. For equilibrium, the clockwise and anticlockwise moments balance. Both gravitational forces contain g, which cancels, leaving known mass times its perpendicular distance equal to unknown mass times its perpendicular distance. Our example scale balances at the fifty centimeter mark. A one hundred gram mass hangs at twenty centimeters, so its lever arm is thirty centimeters. The unknown hangs at seventy centimeters, so its lever arm is twenty centimeters. Unknown mass is one hundred times thirty divided by twenty, or one hundred fifty grams. Pause before using the marks themselves: twenty and seventy are positions, not lever arms. Keep the scale horizontal, account for hanger masses where relevant, and avoid a broad support that lets the pivot position wander. If the pivot is not at the empty scale's center of gravity, its weight adds another torque and must be included. The support force passes through the pivot, so it contributes no torque about that point. This experiment is an application of rotational equilibrium, not a rule that all forces on the scale vanish individually.

chapters.title: Pendulum amplitude reveals energy loss
chapters.formula: Small-angle turning-point energy approximately mg A^2/(2L)
points: Measure successive amplitudes on the same side of the swing.
A squared versus time tracks mechanical-energy decay.
Halving amplitude leaves one quarter of the initial mechanical energy.
chapters.script: A pendulum gradually swings through smaller angles. Instead of merely watching it slow down, we can use amplitude to estimate how its mechanical energy changes. For small angles, with displacement amplitude A measured approximately horizontally and effective length L to the bob's center, the restoring constant is m g divided by L. At a turning point the bob's speed is zero, and its mechanical energy is approximately one half of that constant times A squared. Keep length and bob mass fixed, and energy is proportional to amplitude squared. Record the maximum displacement on the same side after known numbers of oscillations, or at measured times. Square those amplitudes and plot A squared vertically against time horizontally. A decreasing curve shows mechanical energy being transferred to the surroundings through air resistance and friction at the support. Energy is not destroyed; mechanical energy of the pendulum is what decreases. Suppose amplitude falls from eight centimeters to four centimeters. The amplitude ratio is one half, but the energy ratio is one quarter. Seventy-five percent of the initial mechanical energy has been dissipated. Take a moment and separate those percentages. Weak damping with a simple linear resistance model gives approximately exponential amplitude decay, but do not force every measured A-squared graph into a straight line. Avoid drafts, release gently without a push, and use the small-angle approximation. Reading moving turning points has uncertainty, so repeated observations and clear reference marks matter as much as the equation.

chapters.title: Resonance tube: use two lengths
chapters.formula: L1 + e = lambda/4; L2 + e = 3lambda/4; v = 2f(L2 - L1)
points: The water surface acts as the closed end of the air column.
Displacement has a node at the water and an antinode near the open end.
Subtracting successive resonance lengths removes the common end correction.
chapters.script: Let's measure the speed of sound using a tuning fork and a water-filled resonance tube. The water surface forms the closed end of the adjustable air column. Hold the vibrating fork near the open end without touching the tube, and vary the water level slowly to find strong resonance. In the displacement picture, the closed end is a node and the open end is approximately an antinode. The effective open boundary lies slightly beyond the tube mouth, producing an end correction e. The first resonant length satisfies L one plus e equal to one quarter wavelength. The next satisfies L two plus e equal to three quarters wavelength. Subtracting cancels e, so wavelength is twice the difference between the two measured lengths. Multiply by the known fork frequency to get sound speed. Suppose frequency is five hundred hertz, first length sixteen centimeters, and second length fifty centimeters. Their difference is thirty-four centimeters, or zero point three four meters. Wavelength is zero point six eight meters, and speed is three hundred forty meters per second. The same data give end correction of one centimeter, since a quarter wavelength is seventeen centimeters. Pause here: changing the tube length did not change the driving fork frequency. These are two resonant lengths for the same frequency, not a claim that the fork suddenly plays its third harmonic. Repeat resonance positions while raising and lowering the water, record temperature, and distinguish the displacement pattern from the opposite pressure-node pattern.
